The Nature of God in Both Religions

Part II opens here. Before tracing the shared storyline (creation → end), the prior question must be settled: who/what is God in each text? This chapter is built only from the scriptures themselves, read logically, with verse evidence on the table. Tradition is cited only to show how each community read its own text.

Method (per Methodology): claims are sourced to verses; "the tradition says X" is marked as interpretation, not text; every attribute is tested symmetrically.

1. What both texts agree on

Read plainly, the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament, and the Qur'an assert a large shared core:

AttributeBible (sample)Qur'an (sample)
One / uniqueDeut 6:4; Isa 45:5Q 112:1–4; 2:255
Eternal, uncausedPs 90:2Q 57:3 ("the First and the Last")
Creator of allGen 1:1Q 39:62
OmnipotentJer 32:17Q 2:20
OmniscientPs 139:1–4Q 6:59
Sovereign / wills freelyDan 4:35Q 85:16 ("Doer of what He wills")
JustDeut 32:4Q 4:40
MercifulPs 103:8Q 1:1–3 (al-Rahman al-Rahim)
Transcendent, unlike creationIsa 55:8–9Q 42:11 ("nothing like Him")

So the dispute is not "personal creator vs. not." Both affirm one transcendent, omnipotent, just, merciful Creator. The real divergences are sharper and fewer — and they are textual, not vague.

2. The decisive divergences (text + logic)

2.1 Unity: absolutely simple vs. triune

  • Qur'an: unity is numerical and indivisible. Tawhid forbids any internal plurality; Q 112 ("He neither begets nor is born"), Q 4:171 ("do not say 'three'"), Q 5:73. Shirk (association) is the one unforgivable sin (Q 4:48).
  • Bible: one God (Deut 6:4) plus an early high-Christology and triadic strand (John 1:1; Matt 28:19; 2 Cor 13:14) → the Trinity: one essence, three persons.
  • Already adjudicated in Monotheism vs. Trinity: the Qur'an states its unity explicitly; the Bible's triune unity is synthesized, not stated; "1=3" as a bare contradiction fails, but "not plainly biblical, metaphysically heavy" stands.

2.2 Is God relational love by nature?

This is the most underrated textual contrast and deserves the evidence in full.

  • Bible — love is ontologically prior and intrinsic.
  • "*God is love*" — a statement of essence, not just action (1 John 4:8,16).
  • The Father loves the Son "before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24) — i.e., God is loving eternally, independent of creation. On the Trinitarian reading this is logically tidy: love requires a beloved, and the persons supply it within God Himself.
  • Love is shown to the undeserving: Rom 5:8 ("while we were still sinners").
  • Qur'an — mercy is foundational; love is real but largely conditional.
  • Mercy is primary and vast: every chapter but one opens with al-Rahman al-Rahim; "My mercy encompasses all things" (Q 7:156); "Allah has prescribed mercy upon Himself" (Q 6:12).
  • But the verb "Allah loves" is repeatedly conditioned on the recipient's conduct: He loves the doers of good (Q 2:195), the just (Q 5:42), the God-fearing (Q 9:4), the patient (Q 3:146) — and the recurring negative: "Allah does not love the transgressors / the unjust / the arrogant / the corrupters" (Q 2:190; 3:57; 4:36; 5:64; 28:77; and others).
  • Strict transcendence (tanzih) also resists the idea of God needing or being constituted by relation.

Logical reading (no theology imported): on the plain wording, the Bible asserts love as God's essence, prior to and independent of creation and merit; the Qur'an asserts mercy as foundational but love as a response to the worthy. Neither is incoherent. But they make different ontological claims about God's interior life, and the texts say so themselves.

2.3 Fatherhood and self-disclosure

  • Bible: God is Father (Matt 6:9), and His ultimate self- revelation is incarnational — "the Word became flesh" (John 1:14), "he who has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). God can be known by drawing near in a person.
  • Qur'an: fatherhood/begetting is explicitly denied of God (Q 19:88–93; 112:3); God reveals His will via a book and prophets, not by indwelling a human. God is known by His signs (ayat) and names, not by incarnation.
  • Logical note: these are mutually exclusive at the level of mechanism — "God reveals Himself by becoming man" vs. "God categorically does not enter creation." Not an emphasis difference; a contradiction of models. Each is internally consistent on its own terms.

2.4 Forgiveness: by sovereign decree vs. through atonement

  • Qur'an: God forgives directly, by His will, on repentance — "Allah forgives all sins" (Q 39:53); no mediator or sacrifice is required ("no bearer of burdens bears another's burden", Q 35:18).
  • Bible (NT): forgiveness is tied to atonement — "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness" (Heb 9:22); the cross reconciles justice and mercy (Rom 3:25–26).
  • Logical note: this is a structural divergence about how divine justice and mercy relate. Islam: mercy can simply remit, sovereignly. Christianity: a holy God's justice must be satisfied, and substitution satisfies it. Both are coherent systems; they cannot both describe the same God's actual modus operandi.

2.5 Anthropomorphic language and "where" God is

  • Both texts use bodily/spatial language: Bible — God's "hand," "face," "arm," "throne"; Qur'an — God's "hand" (Q 48:10), "face" (Q 55:27), "establishment over the Throne" (istiwa, Q 20:5).
  • Both communities split the same way internally: literalist, metaphorical, and "affirm-without-asking-how" camps.
  • Islam: Mu'tazila (figurative) vs. Ash'ari (bila kayf, "without how") vs. Athari/literal-affirming.
  • Christianity: anthropomorphism as accommodation; the Incarnation as the controlled, intended "localization" of God.
  • Symmetry verdict: the "your scripture is crudely anthropomorphic" jab cuts both ways equally and is a non-argument unless applied evenly (Methodology §3).

2.6 Decree, freedom, and evil

  • Qur'an: strong divine determination — qadar; "Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills" (Q 14:4); yet humans are accountable.
  • Bible: sovereignty (Eph 1:11) held in tension with human responsibility — the very tension that produced the internal Calvinist/Arminian debate.
  • Symmetry verdict: the problem of reconciling omnipotent decree with human freedom is shared, with parallel internal schools on both sides. Neither text "solves" it; neither is uniquely indicted by it.

3. Names as evidence

How a text names God reveals its theology proper:

  • *Qur'an — the 99 Names (al-asma al-husna, Q 7:180; 59:22–24): dominated by sovereignty + mercy: al-Rahman, al-Rahim, al-Malik, al-Quddus, al-Aziz, al-Jabbar, al-Ghaffar*. No name "Father."
  • Hebrew Bible: YHWH (the covenant name, Exod 3:14 "I AM"), El Shaddai, YHWH-Yireh, Qadosh (Holy) — covenantal relationship is built into the naming.
  • New Testament: "Father," "Abba" (Rom 8:15), and divine titles applied to the Son (Kyrios) — naming carries the relational and Trinitarian claim.

The naming sets confirm §2: the Qur'an's God is named for majesty and mercy; the Bible's God is named for covenant and fatherhood.

Arbiter verdict — the nature of God

Present.

  • Shared: one, eternal, omnipotent, omniscient, just, merciful, transcendent Creator — a genuinely large common core.
  • Islamic distinctives: absolute simple unity; mercy foundational; forgiveness by sovereign decree; no incarnation; God known by signs, names, and revelation.
  • Christian distinctives: triune unity; love as God's essence, prior to creation; fatherhood; self-revelation by incarnation; forgiveness through atonement.

Weigh.

  • Strong & textual: the Qur'an's God is more simply and explicitly stated (unity, transcendence) — a real clarity advantage on its own text.
  • Strong & textual: the Bible explicitly predicates love of God's essence and locates it before creation (1 John 4:8; John 17:24) — the Qur'an's own wording instead ties God's love (not mercy) to the recipient's merit (the repeated "Allah does not love…"). This is not apologetic spin; it is what the verbs do in each text.
  • Structural, not cosmetic: incarnation vs. non-incarnation, and atonement vs. sovereign remission, are logically exclusive models — the texts cannot both be describing the same God's actual operation.
  • Symmetric / non-decisive: anthropomorphism and the decree-vs-freedom problem indict neither uniquely.

Judge.

  1. On the shared core: essentially a draw — both texts describe a recognizably overlapping supreme God.
  2. On clarity and parsimony of the God-concept: advantage Qur'an — it states unity and transcendence without needing later metaphysical scaffolding.
  3. On God as intrinsically relational love: advantage Bible — on the plain text, love is God's essence and is pre-creational and unmerited; the Qur'an's text makes God's love conditional while making His mercy foundational. Whether "simpler" or "relationally richer" is the superior trait is a value premise the arbiter cannot adjudicate (Methodology §5).
  4. On forgiveness and self-revelation: not a difference of emphasis but of mechanism — the two cannot both be literally true of one God. Here the arbiter rules only that each model is internally coherent; deciding which is real is a theological-truth question, out of scope.

Bottom line: the two Gods share a wide trunk and diverge on a few load-bearing branches — triunity, intrinsic love, incarnation, mechanism of forgiveness. These are textually demonstrable and mutually exclusive, not mere tonal differences. That is exactly the fault line the chronology (creation → end) will keep re-exposing.
